---

Let me pour my thoughts out on this matter of discussion,
Slow it down—I keep on feeling like I'm rushin',
Like my cousin's dying breaths, or the decision that was made,
But let me backtrack now, let these feelings clear the way.

A normal adolescent, aspiring for the highest,
Chasing goals attainable, determined to be the flyest.
We're all in search of something we have made a pact to do—
The drive of pure ambition, it's in us, it's in you.

Now snatch away each dream that a mother held for her son,
And trade it for a whispered breath: "Baby, just take another one!"
A white man's gun, the very courier of evil—
He left, enjoyed his night, but those gunshots proved lethal.

Deceitful, all the lies we've been told right from the start,
We're more than ghetto thugs—yet these thoughts tear us apart.
What you must understand: our culture rose from oppression,
The Hip Hop deep inside of us, a sacred form of expression.

I wish I had the chance to tell the man who took his life
That the song called "Beef" by Lil Reese should never mark him for the knife.
So is he simply ignorant, or another ghetto thug?
Do you grasp that your own ignorance filled him with three slugs?

I don't want your sympathy, and I don't want affection—
I want to see this country steered in the right direction.
Instead of who the Grammys should be crowning and rewarding,
Let's work to stop the murders—like the one that took my cousin, Jordan.

---

outputs.L3:
# Remembering Jordan

I mourn the loss of my cousin Jordan. He was a normal, ambitious adolescent—no different from any other young person navigating the uncertain path toward adulthood. He had dreams and goals, the kind that were attainable and real, the kind that any of us might hold close to our hearts. He was, in every sense, a boy with a future.

That future was stolen. Jordan was killed by a white man's gun, an act of senseless violence that did more than end a single life. It shattered the dreams a mother held for her son—the hopes she had nurtured since the day he was born, the quiet expectations of watching him grow, succeed, and one day build a life of his own. In an instant, all of it was gone.

I want to speak plainly about something that too many people misunderstand. Hip Hop and Black culture did not emerge as evidence of criminality. They emerged from oppression, rising up as a legitimate and powerful form of expression—a way for a people to speak their truth when so many other avenues were closed to them. This culture is art. It is voice. It is survival. To treat it as proof of wrongdoing is to fundamentally misread its origins and its meaning.

And yet, that is precisely the kind of ignorant assumption that helped kill my cousin. Because he engaged with this culture—because a song could be twisted into supposed evidence that he was a drug dealer—Jordan was wrongly labeled. He was reduced to a stereotype, judged not for who he was but for what others assumed him to be. That assumption, that failure of understanding, contributed to his death.

I am not here to ask for your sympathy. Sympathy changes nothing. What I demand is that this country change its direction. I demand that we prioritize preventing murders like Jordan's over the trivial matters that so often consume our attention. A young life was lost, and countless others remain at risk. It is time we decided that their lives matter more than our comfort, our assumptions, and our indifference.
outputs.L4:
**For Jordan**

They tell me you were seventeen when the music stopped.

Not the music from the speakers—that kept playing, they say, long after the glass shattered and the bass line drowned in the sound of a stranger's fear. I mean the music of you, cousin. The rhythm of your laugh at family cookouts. The way you'd freestyle nonsense in the backseat until Auntie told you to hush. That music. That's what stopped, because a man decided your song was too loud, too Black, too much like a threat he'd already invented in his mind.

He heard Hip Hop and thought he heard a crime.

But let me tell you what he didn't understand, what this whole frightened country refuses to understand: Hip Hop was never a weapon. It was a birth certificate written on the ruins of neighborhoods this nation abandoned. It rose up from the ash of broken promises and burned-out blocks, from young people who had every reason to fall silent and chose instead to *speak*. To rhyme. To make beauty out of what they were handed. That thumping bass wasn't the sound of danger, cousin—it was the sound of survival, of a people saying *we are still here, we are still human, hear us.*

And they heard you. God, how they misheard you.

They looked at your baggy shirt and saw a costume for guilt. They heard your slang and translated it into evidence. They took your youth—that beautiful, unfinished thing—and read it as a sentence already written. The gun was just the period at the end of a lie that had been forming in this country for four hundred years. Somebody pulled a trigger, yes. But the bullet was loaded long before he ever saw your face.

This is what I need this nation to hear:

You are wringing your hands over the wrong things.

You clutch your pearls over the language in a song, over the sag of a young man's jeans, over the volume of his joy—while children like Jordan bleed out in parking lots and driveways and doorways for the crime of existing while Black. You debate whether Hip Hop is "real music" while ignoring whether Black boys are allowed to be real *people*. You are afraid of the art and comfortable with the murder. You have it exactly, tragically backwards.

Ignorance is not harmless. It never was. It is not a quiet thing that stays inside a person's head. It travels. It arms itself. It sits in a car with its window down and its finger curled. Prejudice is not an opinion—it is a loaded thing, and it kills.

So I am not asking for sympathy. I am asking for *change*.

Interrogate the fear you were taught. Ask yourself why a Black teenager's music reads to you as violence, while the violence done to him reads as understandable. Confront the stereotype before it confronts a child. Because every time you let a lie about who we are go unchallenged, you are helping load the gun.

Jordan should be here.

He should be grown now, or growing. He should be arguing with me about lyrics I'm too old to understand. He should be filling a room with that impossible music of his. Instead I am writing this, turning grief into verse the way our people always have—making something that lives out of something that died.

That, too, is Hip Hop, cousin.

That, too, is how we refuse to stay silent.
outputs.L5:
# The Beauty of Taking Things Slow

In a world that constantly pushes us to speed up, there's real wisdom in learning to embrace a **slow** pace. We often feel pressured to rush through our days, but the moments we treasure most are usually the ones where we allowed ourselves to breathe and simply be present.

When you find something you genuinely **like**—whether it's reading a good book, cooking a meal, or spending time with people who matter—resist the urge to hurry through it. The things we enjoy deserve our full attention. A slow morning with a cup of coffee can feel more nourishing than a fast-paced routine that leaves us exhausted before the day even begins.

The key is to **continue** at your own rhythm. Progress doesn't always require speed. In fact, steady and mindful effort often leads to more lasting results than frantic bursts of activity. Whether you're learning a new skill, building a relationship, or working toward a personal goal, the willingness to keep going matters more than how quickly you arrive.

So the next time you feel rushed, give yourself permission to slow down. Do more of what you like, honor your own pace, and continue moving forward—one meaningful step at a time. Life isn't a race to the finish; it's a journey meant to be savored.

**"Empty Chair at Sunday Dinner"**

Yo—

They handed me a folded flag and called it closure,
But there's a hole in my chest where my cousin's laughter used to be.
Thirteen years old, still learning how to tie his shoes proper,
Now he's a headline, a hashtag, a candle at a vigil—
And they wonder why I'm bitter.

See, they blame the culture, point fingers at the beats we make,
Say Hip Hop taught him violence like the mic was the trigger.
But nobody talks about the schools with no books,
The neighborhoods redlined so long the maps forgot to move,
The way they police our skin before they read our names.

Hip Hop didn't kill my cousin.
Hip Hop is the *cry*—
The poets on the corner, the truth they can't deny,
It's Tupac asking questions this country never answers,
It's the drum of a heartbeat trying to survive.

You want to save the children?
Then look me in my eyes.
Stop mourning us in speeches, then voting for our demise.
'Cause every empty chair at every family table
Is a promise that this nation was never quite able—
to see us.

But I'm still here.
And I'll speak until my throat gives out,
For the boy who won't grow up,
For the mothers full of doubt.
This ain't just a verse—
this is a *reckoning*.
Change the country,
or keep counting all the coffins we keep beckoning.

*Rest easy, cuz.*
*I got the mic now.*

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a poem/rap about Jordan Davis, the teenager shot and killed over loud music, exploring themes of oppression, stereotypes, and losing a loved one.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Jordan

**I.**

Seventeen and full of sound,
gas station lights, a Friday found
you laughing loud with all your friends,
not knowing how a young life ends—

not in glory, not in age,
but on some stranger's borrowed rage,
who heard your bass and heard a threat,
a boy he'd never even met.

**II.**

They call it music, called it "thug,"
they built a monster, dug a grave,
before they ever knew your name
or how your mother learned your name

to spell it out at every hearing,
speaking through the tears and fearing
that the world would just move on—
another headline, quickly gone.

**III.**

But we won't let the story fade:
a child was here, a child was made
of everything a father dreams,
of quiet hopes and loud car speakers,

of Sunday mornings, jokes, and light,
of ordinary teenage nights—
until a stereotype was drawn
across your chest, and then you're gone.

**IV.**

So hear me now, this steady drum:
the loud is life, and life should hum.
A Black boy's joy is not a crime,
his volume not a countdown time.

We say his name against the wall
of every one they let just fall—
*Jordan Davis*, seventeen,
the loudest silence in between.

---

*Written in memory of Jordan Davis (1995–2012), and as a reflection on the human cost of prejudice.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a slam poetry piece about the injustice of a young Black man being murdered because of racist assumptions tied to rap music?
counterfactuals.output:
**Loud**

They said the music was too loud.

Too loud.
As if bass could be a weapon,
as if a beat dropping from a rolled-down window
was the same as a hammer cocking back.
They heard a rhythm and imagined a threat—
translated *joy* into *justification*,
turned a teenager's playlist
into a reason to reach.

He was seventeen.
Seventeen and singing along
to somebody else's story
until somebody made him the ending.

See, they never saw the boy.
They saw the *idea* of the boy—
the one they'd been sold on nightly news,
in casting calls for villains,
in every headline that put *thug* in the mouth
of a body that could no longer speak for itself.

They heard the music
and never heard the *him*—
the kid who texted his mama *goodnight*,
the one who had a chemistry test on Monday,
the one whose laugh his little sister
will spend the rest of her life
trying to remember exactly.

Because that's the trick, isn't it?
You make a whole culture into a costume,
then act surprised when someone bleeds
underneath it.
You build the stereotype brick by brick
and call it *self-defense*
when the wall comes down on a child.

*Too loud,* they said.

But I'll tell you what's too loud:
the silence after.
The way the sirens came slow
and the questions came slower.
The way they searched his record
before they searched their conscience.
The way a nation can hear a gunshot
and somehow still ask
what the victim was *wearing,*
what he was *playing,*
what he *did*
to deserve the space between a trigger and a grave.

He didn't do anything.

He turned up the volume on being alive—
and they called that a crime.

So play it loud.
Play it loud at the funeral.
Play it loud in the streets.
Play every song they said was too much,
too Black, too angry, too *there*—
play it until the windows shake,
until the whole world has to feel
what it costs
to make a heartbeat
sound like a threat.

Play it loud.
Because he can't anymore.

And silence
was never safety.
Silence was just
the sound
they wanted us to make.

---

*(A verse for my cousin)*

They put you in a box six feet before your time,
Called it a genre problem, blamed it on the rhyme—
But you was more than music, cuz, you was a whole design,
Every bar you ever spit was survival intertwined.

They don't know where it started, so they don't know what it means,
Don't know the fire in the Bronx or the broken in-between,
Don't know a people robbed of language found a way to speak,
Turned the poverty to poetry, turned the strong from the weak.

We took two turntables and a microphone from dust,
Built cathedrals out of concrete, made a movement out of us—
When they cut the music programs, we became the sound,

The violence is the silence, the neglect across the years,
The violence is the redline, the sentence, and the fear,

They killed you for the image but they bought it by the crate,
Consumed you at a distance, then they left you to your fate,
Sold the sneakers and the slang while they legislated hate—
Cousin, you was culture, and they buried you in shame.

I'm grieving in this pen 'cause the ink is all I got,
They took the man but not the mission, no—they take a lot,
But this music is a fortress and this culture is a knot

So put my flowers on the record, let it spin one more time,
'Cause every empire you built was built on somebody's crime—
